\section[sēricum, sēricī]{sēricum, sēricī — silk}

\label{lesson:LA-C275-sericum}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for loss, then the Latin for a debt.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sēricum, sēricī}
\textbf{sēricum, sēricī} — \textquotedblleft{}silk\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{sēricum} is built on \emph{Sērēs}, \textquotedblleft{}the Seres\textquotedblright{}, the people of the far east whom the Romans knew as makers of silk (Lewis \& Short): the Seric stuff. English \emph{silk} probably comes from the same name.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sēricum, sēricī}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sēricum, sēricī}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{sēricum, sēricī}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for loss, then the Latin for a debt, then say \emph{sēricum, sēricī} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does sēricum, sēricī mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Silk\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[lutum, lutī]{lutum, lutī — mud}

\label{lesson:LA-C275-lutum}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a debt, then the Latin for silk.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: lutum, lutī}
\textbf{lutum, lutī} — \textquotedblleft{}mud\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{lutum} is usually linked with \emph{luō}, \textquotedblleft{}to wash\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), or with a root for dirt seen in \emph{polluō}, \textquotedblleft{}to soil\textquotedblright{}; the details are uncertain. It is a different word from \emph{lūtum}, \textquotedblleft{}a plant used for yellow dye\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for a debt, then the Latin for silk, then say \emph{lutum, lutī} again

\section[pulvis, pulveris]{pulvis, pulveris — dust}

\label{lesson:LA-C275-pulvis}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for silk, then the Latin for mud.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: pulvis, pulveris}
\textbf{pulvis, pulveris} — \textquotedblleft{}dust\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{pulvis} is inherited, usually traced to Proto-Indo-European \emph{*pel-}, \textquotedblleft{}flour, dust\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1); \emph{pollen}, \textquotedblleft{}fine flour\textquotedblright{}, is from the same root. English \emph{powder} comes from \emph{pulvis} through French.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{pulvis, pulveris}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for silk, then the Latin for mud, then say \emph{pulvis, pulveris} again

\section[fūmus, fūmī]{fūmus, fūmī — smoke}

\label{lesson:LA-C275-fumus}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for mud, then the Latin for dust.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: fūmus, fūmī}
\textbf{fūmus, fūmī} — \textquotedblleft{}smoke\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{fūmus} is inherited, usually traced to Proto-Indo-European \emph{*dhuh2mos}, \textquotedblleft{}smoke\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1); Greek \emph{thymos}, \textquotedblleft{}spirit, passion\textquotedblright{}, is a cousin (Lewis \& Short), as is English \emph{dust}.
\end{cousinweb}
